options: A global transaction log
An inverted index mapping terms to document postings
A distributed DBMS wait-for graph
An XML schema for a crawler’s configuration
explanation: An inverted index associates terms with document identifiers, allowing candidate retrieval without scanning every page. Link-structure indexes instead represent hyperlinks, and transaction logs and wait-for graphs solve unrelated consistency problems.
question: A Web search engine must quickly find documents containing the term "replication". Which data structure is most directly suited to this operation?

options: Because HTML cannot contain database data
Because crawlers follow discoverable URLs and may not generate the required form queries or access private interfaces
Because inverted indexes cannot represent words from dynamic pages
Because the content necessarily belongs to the dark Web
explanation: The hidden/deep Web can require submitting form parameters or invoking APIs to reveal results. A crawler following linked pages alone cannot enumerate arbitrary source queries; deep Web does not imply the dark Web or an index-format limitation.
question: A university site exposes millions of records only as results of submitting search forms, with no links to every result. Why does ordinary link-based crawling miss much of this data?

options: Shredding XML into relations
Applying PageRank to XML nodes
Updating every RDF replica
Using one-copy serializability to publish XML
explanation: XML shredding maps document content and (as necessary) structure into relational tables. XML publishing/composing goes in the opposite direction, generating XML from database contents; a native XML store preserves documents as first-class data.
question: A relational DBMS parses incoming XML documents and distributes their elements, attributes and identifiers among relational tables. What does this operation describe?

options: RDF facts are subject–predicate–object triples forming a labeled graph, whereas XML naturally stores an ordered element hierarchy
RDF is necessarily a table with exactly three columns on disk
XML cannot represent relationships between objects
RDF subjects must always be plain text literals
explanation: RDF defines a logical graph of triples, independent of one physical storage layout. XML primarily models nested ordered document structure; it may encode references, so claiming that XML can never represent relationships is too strong.
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes RDF from a typical XML tree?

options: SELECT ?s WHERE { ?s <urn:studiesAt> <urn:uio> . }
SELECT ?s WHERE { ?s <urn:uio> <urn:studiesAt> . }
SELECT ?s WHERE { <urn:uio> <urn:studiesAt> ?s . }
SELECT ?s WHERE { ?s <urn:studiesAt> <urn:other> . }
explanation: The first SPARQL triple pattern uses the correct subject variable, predicate urn:studiesAt and object urn:uio; it binds ?s to student 7. The other patterns reverse predicate/object or select the other student.
question: An RDF graph contains (urn:student:7, urn:studiesAt, urn:uio) and (urn:student:8, urn:studiesAt, urn:other). Which query pattern finds only student 7?

options: A subject-centered property table containing those columns
A single unindexed triple table, guaranteed to outperform every alternative
A collection of unrelated XML files without an index
A global wait-for graph reused as an RDF index
explanation: Grouping co-occurring predicates into a property table permits many same-subject values to be retrieved together, often reducing star-query joins. Sparse or multivalued properties can make such tables inefficient, so it is not an unconditional winner.
question: Most RDF queries request name, email and department for the same subject (a star pattern). What physical layout may avoid repeated joins when the properties usually occur together?
Given the XML document in the code block, which XPath expression selects the title element of the book whose id is b2?
options: /catalog/book[@id='b2']/title
/catalog/title[@id='b2']
/catalog/book/title[@id='b1']
//book/@title
explanation: The correct path descends through catalog/book, filters the book element on its id attribute with [@id='b2'], then selects its title child. XPath navigates document hierarchy; @title would refer to an attribute, not the title element.
source: Özsu & Valduriez (2020), Ch. 12 §12.6.2 (XML path/query languages); Lecture 6 slides 23–26 introduce XML documents.
